newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma signs top reformer's resignation.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma signs top reformer's resignation.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Monday accepted the resignation of Viktor Pynzenyk, the former Soviet republic's top reformist politician who quit in anger five days ago.
"The president signed the deputy prime minister's resignation offer at the insistence of Viktor Mikhailovich (Pyzenyk)," Tamara Kutsai, the former minister's spokeswoman, told Reuters.

A spokeswoman for Kuchma's press service said the president had not yet signed a decree on the resignation but a spokesman for the former minister said the decision had been approved and Pynzenyk would hold a news conference at 6 p.m. (1500 GMT).

Last Wednesday an aide said Pynzenyk had offered to resign as deputy prime minister in charge of economic reform because he was "extremely unhappy" with the way Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko's government was handling reforms.

The president's press service said three days ago that Kuchma, in line with the constitution, had ordered Lazarenko to decide on the offer by Pynzenyk, a leading reformer popular with Western funding bodies.

The president on Saturday again blamed Lazarenko for the absence of a budget and a tax reform package to underpin it, which would help pave the way for a multi-billion-dollar loan from the International Monetary Fund.
"I am convinced that if the government paid attention to passing the budget then it would be passed," Kuchma said.

Kuchma said the budget deficit would be six percent of gross domestic product, half of which was to be covered by foreign credits. "But there are none, and there won't be any until we pass the budget. Then what will we do, start up the printing presses again? Then the whole economy would collapse".
Pynzenyk has repeatedly criticised the government and parliament for dragging their heels in implementing stringent reform measures to pull Ukraine out of economic decline.
"Thumbs up to Pynzenyk for showing some backbone," one Western analyst said of the decision by the reformer, seen with central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko as the guardian of reforms in Ukraine.

He added: "I think he was getting a bit tired of being the figleaf" concealing the reality of Ukraine's economy, which has been in stubborn decline in the five years since it won independence from Moscow.
